Register geoarrowrs functions with Arrow

Source: R/arrow.R
register_geoarrow_udfs.Rd

Makes geoarrowrs functions callable inside dplyr verbs on an Arrow Table, RecordBatch, or Dataset, so you never have to pull the geometry into R.

Usage

register_geoarrow_udfs(crs = NULL, functions = NULL, prefix = "")

Arguments

crs

the coordinate reference system the kernels dispatch on. Pass NULL, the default, for data with no CRS, a CRS string, or any object carrying one: an Arrow Table, RecordBatch, Dataset, Schema, Array, or a GeoArrow array or vector. Pass a list to cover several at once

functions

names of geoarrowrs functions to register, or NULL, the default, for every function register_geoarrow_udfs() supports

prefix

a string to prepend to each registered name, to avoid masking an existing Arrow binding

Value

the registered names, invisibly

Details

Arrow's query engine only knows the kernels you register with it, so when you call a geoarrowrs function on a Table, Arrow warns that it does not support the expression and pulls the data into R instead. register_geoarrow_udfs() registers each function as an Arrow scalar kernel, so the engine runs it and, on a Dataset, streams it batch by batch without ever holding the whole column in memory.

register_geoarrow_udfs() registers per CRS, not per table. It registers a kernel for every GeoArrow geometry type, so one call covers points, linestrings, polygons, and their multi variants at once. It registers no kernel for a type a function cannot handle, such as ga_length_euclidean() on polygons.

It registers the arguments that are not geometry too. Numeric arguments such as the epsilon of ga_simplify() take a double column or a literal, which the kernel recycles row by row. Option arguments such as the metric of ga_densify() take a literal string. Arrow has no optional arguments, so you must pass every argument of a registered function.

It does not register ga_unary_union(), ga_explode(), or ga_flatten(), because they change the length of the array and a scalar kernel may not.

It also registers kernels for a bare binary column of WKB, which is what plain Parquet writes. The kernel parses the WKB and returns a geometry result as WKB, since a kernel's output type cannot depend on what the column holds. To work on native GeoArrow instead, cast once with ga_as_point() or one of its siblings and follow it with compute(). Without the compute(), Arrow inlines the cast into each expression that reads it and runs it once per use rather than once per column.

A GeoArrow type carries its CRS, and Arrow compares it when it looks for a kernel, so you have to pass a crs that matches the data. Pass every CRS you need in one call: when you register a name again, register_geoarrow_udfs() replaces the kernels it had.

geoarrowrs calls register_geoarrow_udfs() once with crs = NULL when it loads, so you can use data with no CRS without any setup. For data with a CRS, you still need to call it with that CRS. Set options(geoarrowrs.register_udfs = FALSE) before loading to skip the call, which also keeps geoarrowrs from loading arrow when it loads.

Examples

library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: ‘dplyr’
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’:
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

nc <- as.data.frame(read_shapefile(
  system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf")
))
tbl <- arrow::arrow_table(nc)

register_geoarrow_udfs(crs = tbl)

tbl |>
  mutate(area = ga_unsigned_area(geometry)) |>
  select(NAME, area) |>
  head(3) |>
  collect()
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   NAME        area
#>   <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 Ashe      0.114 
#> 2 Alleghany 0.0614
#> 3 Surry     0.143
